adjudication_records.issue_text: assignment_source.to_dict() returns a dict containing datetime objects which is passed as Celery task kwargs; the default JSON serializer raises EncodeError, so assignee sync fails to enqueue and propagation is silently dropped

AssignmentSource dataclass uses timezone.now() as a class-definition-time default, so every instance gets the process-start timestamp instead of actual queuing time; should use field(default_factory=timezone.now)
from_dict never validates types, so after JSON round-trip queued arrives as an ISO string and AssignmentSource.queued becomes a str instead of datetime, violating the dataclass contract

adjudication.rationale: In `AssignmentSource.from_dict`, the code simply does `return cls(**input_dict)` and only guards against `ValueError`/`TypeError`, so it does not enforce that `queued` is a `datetime` (it will accept any object for `queued`, including a `str`). The diff also shows `to_dict()` uses `asdict(self)`, which includes `queued`, and that dict is passed through a background task boundary (`assignment_source_dict` in `sync_assignee_outbound`). However, the claim that a “JSON round-trip” will specifically produce an ISO string is not directly shown in the diff (depends on task serialization), and `queued` is not used anywhere in the shown changes, so the impact is not a clearly verifiable breakage from this diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: AssignmentSource dataclass default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at module import, so all instances without an explicit value carry a stale import-time timestamp, and the test only asserts non-None so it passes vacuously

adjudication.rationale: In `AssignmentSource` the field is defined as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`, which calls `timezone.now()` at class definition/import time, so every instance created without an explicit `queued` will share the same stale timestamp. This is a real correctness issue and should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead. The added test `test_to_dict` only asserts `queued` is non-None, so it would not detect this problem.

matched_golden_ids: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.

This is the same underlying issue as the golden comment about serializer-dependent JSON failures due to a datetime in kwargs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No test exercises the real inbound path (sync_group_assignee_inbound) that produces the AssignmentSource; the integration_id identity link that makes cycle prevention work is only tested with a hand-built object

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new cycle-prevention logic that relies on `AssignmentSource` being created on the inbound path (`sync_group_assignee_inbound` now passes `assignment_source=AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)` into `GroupAssignee.objects.assign/deassign`). The new/updated tests exercise cycle prevention only by directly calling `GroupAssignee.objects.assign(..., assignment_source=AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration))` (hand-constructed source) and asserting `ExampleIntegration.sync_assignee_outbound` is not called, rather than driving it through `sync_group_assignee_inbound` to confirm the integration_id linkage is propagated end-to-end into the outbound task and `installation.should_sync(..., sync_source)` check. This is a specific missing-coverage issue for the newly added nontrivial behavior, not a proven functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Deassign cycle-prevention is entirely untested; no test asserts that a deassign originating from the same integration is suppressed, and this path can regress independently

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds cycle-prevention via `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync(..., sync_source)` returning False when `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id`, and this is used by the outbound assignee task for both assign and unassign (`sync_assignee_outbound` calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` regardless of `assign`). A test was added for the assign case (`test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration`), but there is no analogous test covering the unassign/deassign path (e.g., `GroupAssignee.objects.deassign(..., assignment_source=AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration))` resulting in `mock_sync_assignee_outbound` not being called). Thus the finding about missing deassign cycle-prevention testing is accurate and diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: from_dict silently swallows malformed payloads by returning None, which means should_sync skips the cycle check entirely — a fail-open design that can re-enable infinite sync loops; should at minimum log or alert

adjudication.rationale: In `sync_assignee_outbound`, `assignment_source_dict` is parsed via `AssignmentSource.from_dict(...)`, which returns `None` on malformed input. That `None` is then passed into `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)`, and in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync(...)` the cycle-prevention guard only runs when `sync_source` is truthy. So an invalid/malformed payload effectively disables the new cycle check and falls back to config-based syncing. The diff doesn’t show this happening in normal code paths (it uses `assignment_source.to_dict()`), so it’s more of a robustness/observability concern (e.g., logging or failing closed when a dict is present but invalid) than a clearly triggered defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Inbound change from one linked issue now suppresses outbound assign/unassign propagation to sibling issues on the same integration (e.g., a Jira ticket and its duplicate linked to the same group), a silent behavior regression with no test or stated acceptance criterion

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly introduces cycle-prevention logic that suppresses outbound assignee sync when the change source is the same integration (`IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync(...): if sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id: return False`) and wires inbound assignments to pass that source (`sync_group_assignee_inbound` passes `AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)` into `GroupAssignee.assign/deassign`). This behavior is not “silent”/untested: a new test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` asserts `sync_assignee_outbound` is not called when `assignment_source` matches the target integration, matching the intended behavior described by the inline comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Status-sync cycle prevention is not addressed: sync_status_outbound gained an assignment_source parameter but no implementation or status-inbound path creates or checks a source, making it dead plumbing and leaving resolve/unresolve loops unprotected

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds generic cycle-prevention support via `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync(..., sync_source=...)` (it now returns False when `sync_source.integration_id` matches `self.org_integration.integration_id`), and threads `AssignmentSource` through the *assignee* outbound path (`sync_group_assignee_outbound` -> task -> `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` and into `sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=...)`). However, for status syncing the diff only changes the abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature to accept `assignment_source`, but shows no call-site updates to pass a source and no status-inbound/outbound logic that checks/constructs a source for status changes. So, as shown, status cycle prevention is not implemented (the new parameter is effectively unused plumbing in this diff), leaving resolve/unresolve loops unaddressed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: sync_assignee_outbound task unconditionally passes assignment_source kwarg to provider implementations whose signatures don't accept it, causing TypeError and breaking all outbound assignee sync

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show `sync_assignee_outbound` now calling `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)` (tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py), but the PR diff does not show the signature of provider implementations nor the base/mixin `sync_assignee_outbound` method signature. Therefore, the claim that this will cause a `TypeError` and “break all outbound assignee sync” cannot be verified from the diff alone (providers may already accept `**kwargs`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: AssignmentSource.queued uses timezone.now() as a dataclass default evaluated once at import time, so all instances record module import time instead of queue time

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py`, the dataclass field is defined as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`. Because `timezone.now()` is *called* at class definition/import time, that single datetime value becomes the shared default for all `AssignmentSource()` instances created without an explicit `queued`, so they will all record the module import time rather than the actual creation/queue time. This should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

adjudication_records.issue_text: assignment_source.to_dict() puts a raw datetime into Celery task kwargs, which raises an encode error under JSON serialization so the sync task never enqueues

adjudication.rationale: In `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` the dataclass is converted via `asdict(self)`, which will include the `queued: datetime` field as a raw `datetime` object (see `src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py`). That dict is then passed directly into Celery task kwargs as `assignment_source_dict` in `sync_group_assignee_outbound` (`apply_async(..., kwargs={..., "assignment_source_dict": assignment_source.to_dict() ...})`). If the Celery serializer is JSON (a common/default configuration), raw `datetime` objects are not JSON-serializable and will raise an encoding/serialization error at enqueue time. The diff shows no datetime-to-string conversion before enqueueing, so the finding is grounded in the new code path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: from_dict silently returns None on ValueError/TypeError, so deserialization failure disables sync-cycle prevention and allows the sync loop the feature is meant to prevent

adjudication.rationale: Diff shows `AssignmentSource.from_dict()` returns `None` on `ValueError`/`TypeError` (missing/unexpected keys), and `sync_assignee_outbound` then passes that `None` into `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)`. Since `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` only blocks cycles when `sync_source` is non-`None` and matches the integration id, a deserialization failure would indeed bypass the new cycle-prevention guard and fall back to config-based syncing. However, the diff also shows `assignment_source_dict` is produced internally via `assignment_source.to_dict()` (which includes required keys), so this is primarily a robustness/“fail open” concern for malformed task kwargs rather than a demonstrable defect in normal flow from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: sync_status_outbound abstract signature gains an assignment_source parameter with no call sites or producers, adding dead surface every provider must carry

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the abstract method signature in `IssueSyncIntegration.sync_status_outbound` to include `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` (issues.py, lines ~400+), but this diff only produces/passes assignment source data for assignee syncing (`GroupAssignee` -> `sync_group_assignee_outbound` -> celery task -> `installation.sync_assignee_outbound`). There are no status-sync call sites in this diff that pass or even construct an `AssignmentSource` for `sync_status_outbound`, so the new parameter is currently unused surface area that implementers may need to accommodate (especially for typed overrides), without delivering behavior here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: AssignmentSource.source_name is written and serialized but never read by any code, making it unused scope expansion

adjudication.rationale: In this diff, `AssignmentSource.source_name` is set in `AssignmentSource.from_integration()` and included in `to_dict()`/`from_dict()`, but the only behavioral use of `AssignmentSource` shown is in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync(...)`, which checks only `sync_source.integration_id` against `self.org_integration.integration_id`. No code in the diff reads `source_name` for logic, so it is currently unused beyond serialization/tests, representing scope/field expansion without demonstrated need.

adjudication_records.issue_text: queued: datetime = timezone.now() is a dataclass field default evaluated once at module import, so every AssignmentSource gets process startup time instead of actual queue time

adjudication.rationale: In `AssignmentSource` (new file `src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py`), the dataclass field is defined as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`. This calls `timezone.now()` at class definition/import time, so all instances that rely on the default will share the same timestamp (process startup time) instead of the actual instantiation/queue time. Dataclasses require `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` to compute per-instance defaults.

adjudication_records.issue_text: assignment_source.to_dict() puts a raw datetime object into Celery task kwargs, causing serialization failure and TypeError with old-signature workers during rolling deploys, breaking assignee outbound sync org-wide

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new Celery task kwarg `assignment_source_dict` to `sync_assignee_outbound` and always includes it in `apply_async` (even when `assignment_source` is None): `kwargs={..., "assignment_source_dict": ...}` in `src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py`. During a rolling deploy, any old workers still running the previous task signature (without this kwarg) would receive an unexpected keyword argument and raise `TypeError`, breaking outbound assignee sync. Additionally, when `assignment_source` is provided, `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` uses `dataclasses.asdict()` and includes `queued` as a raw `datetime` (`queued: datetime = timezone.now()`), which can be non-serializable depending on the Celery serializer configuration.

adjudication_records.issue_text: from_dict returns None on malformed payload and should_sync then skips the cycle check entirely, failing open with no log, metric, or error

adjudication.rationale: In `sync_assignee_outbound`, the task payload is parsed via `AssignmentSource.from_dict(...)`, which returns `None` on missing/invalid keys (see `from_dict` catching `ValueError`/`TypeError`). That `None` is then passed into `installation.should_sync(...)`, and the cycle-prevention check (`if sync_source and sync_source.integration_id == ...`) is skipped when `sync_source` is `None`, so outbound sync proceeds with no log/metric/error about the malformed payload. This is a real edge-case/observability gap grounded in the diff, but it’s not clearly a correctness defect because allowing `None` preserves backward compatibility for callers that don’t send an assignment source.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Cycle check only blocks re-entry into the same integration_id, so cross-integration ping-pong loops (e.g. Jira ↔ GitHub through Sentry) are unbroken

adjudication.rationale: The new cycle guard in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync(..., sync_source)` only returns `False` when `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id` (see `issues.py`). That prevents re-entry into the same integration, but explicitly “still allow[s] other integrations to propagate changes outward,” so an assignment sourced from Integration A can still sync outbound to Integration B, and vice versa. The diff does not implement any broader loop-prevention across multiple integrations (e.g., tracking a chain or suppressing re-broadcasts), so cross-integration ping-pong remains possible as an architectural/edge-case concern rather than a verifiable defect against the stated intent in the comment.

adjudication_records.issue_text: assignment_source parameter added to abstract sync_status_outbound has no caller in the diff; status sync cannot participate in cycle prevention and the parameter is dead surface

adjudication.rationale: The diff updates the abstract method signature `IssueSyncIntegration.sync_status_outbound(..., assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None, **kwargs)` but does not update any status-sync call sites in the shown changes to pass or use `assignment_source`. In contrast, assignee sync is wired end-to-end (task kwarg `assignment_source_dict` -> `AssignmentSource.from_dict` -> `installation.should_sync(..., parsed_assignment_source)` -> `sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=...)`). Within this diff, status sync has no analogous propagation, so the new parameter is currently unused surface and cycle-prevention based on source integration is not applied to status sync here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: should_sync signature change on widely-subclassed IssueBasicIntegration/IssueSyncIntegration ABC breaks subclasses overriding the old two-argument should_sync with TypeError

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `IssueBasicIntegration.should_sync` / `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync` to accept an extra optional parameter (`sync_source: AssignmentSource | None = None`) and updates call sites to pass it (e.g. `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` in `sync_assignee_outbound.py`). In Python, if any concrete integration installation class overrides `should_sync` with the old signature `(self, attribute)` and does not accept the new argument (or `**kwargs`), this new call will raise `TypeError: ... takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given`. The diff does not update any other subclasses, so this is a real compatibility risk introduced by the change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Test mocks the provider's sync_assignee_outbound installation method instead of exercising the changed Celery task signature and to_dict/from_dict round-trip, and assert_called_with compares a fresh RPC call result rather than identity

adjudication.rationale: The updated GroupAssignee tests *do* exercise the changed Celery task path and the AssignmentSource dict round-trip. GroupAssignee.objects.assign/deassign calls sync_group_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=...), which enqueues sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async with the new kwarg `assignment_source_dict` built via `assignment_source.to_dict()` (src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py). In the task, that dict is parsed via `AssignmentSource.from_dict(...)` and then passed into `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` (src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py). The new test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` relies on this parsing to prevent sync-cycles (it would fail if the signature/round-trip weren’t working). Separately, `tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py` explicitly tests `to_dict`/`from_dict`. The comment about `assert_called_with` using a fresh `user_service.get_user(...)` is true but is not a verifiable defect from the diff and is more of a stylistic brittleness note.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Mutable dataclass field default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` in assignment_source.py:14 is evaluated once at import time, so every AssignmentSource carries the process-start timestamp instead of the actual enqueue time

adjudication.rationale: In `AssignmentSource` the dataclass field is defined as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` (new file `assignment_source.py`). In Python dataclasses, that expression is evaluated once when the class is defined (import time), so all `AssignmentSource` instances will get the same process-start timestamp instead of a per-instance “now”. This should use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` to capture creation/enqueue time per instance.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New required kwarg assignment_source_dict added to a queued Celery task signature without versioning causes rolling-deploy skew: old workers raise TypeError on the unexpected keyword argument and drop assignee sync until all workers update

During a rolling deploy, old workers still running the previous task function signature (without `assignment_source_dict`) would receive this unexpected kwarg and raise `TypeError`, dropping those queued assignee-sync tasks until workers are updated.
